## Introduction

Irrigation management is one of the most important factors influencing wheat yield and quality in the Pacific Northwest. Wheat yield potential is determined by three key components: the number of heads per unit area, the number of kernels per head, and the average grain weight. These yield components are influenced by water availability at different growth stages.  

Moisture stress at any growth stage before the grain soft dough phase can reduce wheat yields; however, adequate soil moisture during the tillering and boot-to-flowering stages has the most significant impact on yield components. Drought conditions during the tillering and boot-to-flowering stages may lead to reduced head formation, kernel number, and, ultimately, the greatest yield reductions.  

Effective irrigation scheduling is essential for optimizing yield and water use efficiency. Irrigation scheduling determines the amount of water to apply and aligns water applications with crop requirements in a timely manner. Efficient scheduling requires knowledge of crop water use (evapotranspiration) and plant-available soil moisture, which is based on soil water holding capacities. The next three subsections provide guidance on crop water use, soil water holding capacity, and irrigation systems and scheduling for irrigated wheat production systems in the Pacific Northwest.

## Soil Available Water-Holding Capacity

### Available Water-holding Capacity of Soil

The amount of water a soil will store for crop use is called the available water-holding capacity (AWHC) and is typically expressed as inches of water per foot of soil depth (inches/foot). AWHC is determined by the soil’s texture, structure, and organic matter content, all of which influence the ability of soil to retain moisture in a form available to plants.  

Available water-holding capacities vary widely among soil texture types found in the Pacific Northwest. Loamy soils usually have AWHC values above 2 inches/foot, making them ideal to support consistent crop growth. Sandy soils typically hold less than 1 inch of available water per foot due to their larger pore spaces and lower surface area. Sandy loam soils generally fall somewhere in between these two extremes and are common in many irrigated agricultural regions of the Pacific Northwest.  

Available water-holding capacities for most agricultural soil series found in southern Idaho are listed in Table 10. For more detailed site-specific information, consult University of Idaho CIS 236, Available Water-holding Capacities of Soils in Southern Idaho, which provides AWHC estimates of soils where irrigated wheat is commonly grown. 
The AWHC of a soil profile varies with depth, as soil texture at different depths can vary considerably throughout the root zone. To calculate the total AWHC of a field for wheat production, first determine the thickness and texture of each soil layer within the effective root zone, which is typically around 3 feet for wheat. Then, apply the AWHC value for each layer to estimate total water storage. For example, a soil profile that is sandy in the top foot but transitions to sandy loam in the second and third feet will have different water-holding characteristics in each layer. An example calculation is shown in Table 11.  

If you are interested in determining the AWHC for a specific field or location, the [USDA Web Soil Survey](https://websoilsurvey.nrcs.usda.gov/app/WebSoilSurvey.aspx) is a valuable resource.  

Total AWHC of a soil profile represents the total available soil moisture (ASM) in inches between irrigation events that is available for crop uptake. Understanding ASM is essential for setting appropriate irrigation thresholds and avoiding under- and over-irrigation.  

### Determining Available Soil Moisture

Available soil moisture can be determined through direct measurement of soil water content or estimated using crop evapotranspiration (ET) values from local weather data. Direct measurements of ASM include:  

-	Soil feel and appearance (manual evaluation)  
-	Gravimetric sampling (weighing samples before and after oven drying)  
-	Soil moisture sensors such as tensiometers, time-domain reflectometry (TDR), or capacitance probes.  

One of the most practical methods of estimating soil moisture depletion is called the “water budget” or “checkbook” method (see [PNW 288, Irrigation Scheduling](https://hdl.handle.net/2376/7117), and University of Idaho MS 39, Soil Moisture Scheduling Card). Once the soil has drained to field capacity (generally 1 to 2 days after full irrigation), further losses of soil moisture occur primarily through ET. If the AWHC of the full soil profile and the amount of soil moisture lost to ET each day are known, then ASM can be estimated by subtracting the sum of the daily ET values from the initial soil water content.  

Today, ET data are widely available through state and regional weather networks (e.g. AgriMet and OpenET), on-farm weather stations (e.g. METER Group, Davis Instruments, Campbell Scientific, etc.), and irrigation scheduling tools. Remember, while water budgets provide useful estimates of soil moisture depletion, periodic field-based measurements (using soil moisture sensors or manual checks) are recommended to validate estimates for more accuracy.
